newsitem.title: CANADA: Stranded Canadian anglers rescued successfully.
newsitem.headline: Stranded Canadian anglers rescued successfully.

text.p: Police and military crews using boats and helicopters successfully concluded their rescue on Sunday afternoon of hundreds of anglers trapped on ice floes on Lake Simcoe, about 45 miles (70 km) north of Toronto.
But some remained on the ice, refusing help, police said.
"There were some that wanted to keep fishing," York Region police Constable Charles Kean said.
While most ice fishers have heated huts and supplies to fend off cold, police said the ice was considered dangerous and needed a prolonged cold with no wind to freeze up again.
"We are urging people to stay off the ice surface as it is extremely unsafe at this point," Ontario Provincial Police Sergeant Dana Morris said from Orillia, near Lake Simcoe.

Several huge cracks broke through the thick ice on Lake Simcoe on Saturday afternoon during an ice-fishing derby, stranding at least 700 people on the ice. One crack was more than seven miles (11 kms) long and at least 300 feet (100 metres) wide in some spots.

Emergency crews from three police forces and the military used helicopters, military planes, hovercraft and boats to bring people ashore on Saturday, but poor visibility from snow squalls and high winds forced the rescuers to close down their operations during the night, police said.

About 200 people spent a cold, windy night in fishing huts on the ice floes, officials said. By Sunday morning, helicopters and boats were able to rescue anyone left who wanted to be rescued, Kean said.
One person was taken to a hospital on Sunday morning with hypothermia after a van full of people tried to drive across the ice and tipped forward into a fissure, local radio stations reported.
The front end of the van was submerged, throwing the passengers to the front of the vehicle, but they managed to escape by breaking windows and climbing out.
No other injuries were reported by police.

While the ice was about eight inches (20 cms) thick in most places and had been considered safe enough for fishing and even driving on, strong currents and vicious winds pushed large pieces of ice away from the shore, explained Morris.
"This is a rather freak situation," he said. "The winds drove the ice floes from the main portion of the ice."
